No people made a more formidable appearance in warlike array than the Romans. “Understanding dark sentences.” Moses, in the scripture just referred to says, “Whose tongue thou shalt not understand.” This could not be said of the Babylonians, Persians, or Greeks, in reference to the Jews; for the Chaldean and Greek languages were used to a greater or less extent in Palestine. This was not the case, however, with the Latin.

“When the transgressors are come to the full.” All along, the connection between God’s people and their oppressors is 182 kept in view. It was on account of the transgressions of his people that they were sold into captivity. And their continuance in sin brought more and more severe punishment. At no time were the Jews more corrupt, morally, as a nation, than at the time they came under the jurisdiction of the Romans.

“Mighty, but not by his own power.” The success of the Romans was owing largely to the aid of their allies, and divisions among their enemies, of which they were ever ready to take advantage.

“He shall destroy wonderfully.” The Lord told the Jews by the prophet Ezekiel that he would deliver them to men who were “skilful to destroy.” How full of meaning is such a description, and how applicable to the Romans! In taking Jerusalem, they slew eleven hundred thousand Jews, and made ninety-seven thousand captives. So wonderfully did they destroy this once mighty and holy people.

And what they could not accomplish by force, they secured by artifice. Their flatteries, fraud, and corruption were as fatal as their thunderbolts of war. And Rome, finally, in the person of one of its governors, stood up against the Prince of princes, by giving sentence of death against Jesus Christ. “But he shall be broken without hand,” an expression which identifies the destruction of this power with the smiting of the image of chapter 2.

VERSE 26. And the vision of the evening and the morning which was told is true; wherefore shut thou up the vision; for it shall be for many days. 27. And I Daniel fainted, and was sick certain days; afterward I rose up, and did the king’s business; and I was astonished at the vision, but none understood it.

“The vision of the evening and the morning,” is that of the 2300 days. In view of the long period of oppression, and the calamities which were to come upon his people, Daniel fainted, and was sick certain days. He was astonished at the vision, but did not understand it. Why did not Gabriel at this time fully carry out his instructions, and cause Daniel to understand the vision? — Because Daniel had received all that he could then bear. Further instruction is therefore deferred to a future time.

keyPoints.label: Ram = Medo-Persia, with the higher horn last (Persia)
keyPoints.detail: Per verse 20, the ram with two horns is the kings of Media and Persia; the two horns are the two nationalities, and the higher horn coming up last is the Persian element, which began as a mere ally of the Medes but became the leading division of the empire.

keyPoints.label: He-goat = Grecia; notable horn = Alexander, broken at his peak
keyPoints.detail: Per verse 21, the rough goat is the kingdom of Grecia, coming from the west; the notable horn between his eyes is the first king, Alexander the Great, who overthrew Persia (Granicus, Issus, Arbela) and whose horn was broken in the very prime of its strength.

keyPoints.label: Four horns = Alexander's four successor divisions
keyPoints.detail: When the great horn was broken, within fifteen years exactly four notable horns arose toward the four winds: Cassander (west/Macedonia), Lysimachus (north/Thrace and Asia Minor), Seleucus (east/Syria and Babylon), and Ptolemy (south/Egypt) — none with the original kingdom's power.

keyPoints.label: Little horn is Rome, not Antiochus Epiphanes
keyPoints.detail: Smith refutes the Antiochus view — he was only one of twenty-six Syrian kings, illustrious in name only, never exceeding great, made to evacuate Egypt and pay tribute to Rome, and died about 164 years before Christ. The little horn instead fits Rome, which succeeded Grecia as the exceeding-great fourth power and stood up against the Prince of princes by crucifying Christ.

keyPoints.label: Rome's two phases: pagan and papal
keyPoints.detail: The little horn symbolizes Rome's entire history in two phases — pagan Rome ('the daily') remodeled into papal Rome ('the transgression of desolation'). The papacy casts down truth, makes war on the saints, prospers for its allotted time, and is finally broken without hand at Christ's second coming.

keyPoints.label: 'Daily' means continual/paganism, not a sacrifice
keyPoints.detail: Smith argues 'sacrifice' is a wrongly supplied word; the Hebrew means 'continual.' Because the question 'How long the vision?' implies a long series of years, the 'daily' must be an enduring desolating power — paganism — paired with the papal 'transgression of desolation,' the two phases of opposition to God's work.

keyPoints.label: Sanctuary to be cleansed is the heavenly tabernacle
keyPoints.detail: After ruling out the earth, the land of Canaan, and the church, Smith concludes the sanctuary is the true tabernacle in heaven (Hebrews 8-9) of which the Mosaic tabernacle was a type. Its cleansing — a removal of sin by blood (Christ's), not by fire — is the closing work of Christ as High Priest, timed by the 2300 days, whose start is explained in Daniel 9.
